text:
Genesis 22 rewards attention to what is wanting in it. Sarah does not appear anywhere in the chapter, and the book announces her death in the verse immediately following; the scene implies, without stating, that something in the household did not survive the events on the mountain. Abraham returns to the servants; Isaac is not mentioned. The narrative turns away at exactly the point where a lesser story would linger, and its silence is not mere absence, but testimony.

It may be answered that the chapter simply follows the conventions of ancient narrative, which rarely reports the feelings of characters and never explains. This, perhaps, in some sense, may be allowed to be arguably true. Yet the narrator elsewhere reports what characters feel: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps. The reticence here is deliberate; there is in the text an awareness of what is being withheld. Restraint, in this narrative voice, is a kind of accusation.
